{{Short description|Topological space construction}}
{{distinguish|Quotient space (linear algebra)}}

[[Image:Disk to Sphere using Quotient Space.gif|thumb|Illustration of the construction of a [[topological sphere]] as the quotient space of a [[Disk (mathematics)|disk]], by ''gluing'' together to a single point the points (in blue) of the boundary of the disk.]]
In [[topology]] and related areas of [[mathematics]], the '''quotient space''' of a [[topological space]] under a given [[equivalence relation]] is a new topological space constructed by endowing the [[quotient set]] of the original topological space with the '''quotient topology''', that is, with the [[finest topology]] that makes [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]] the [[canonical projection map]] (the function that maps points to their [[equivalence class]]es). In other words, a subset of a quotient space is [[Open set|open]] if and only if its [[preimage]] under the canonical projection map is open in the original topological space.

Intuitively speaking, the points of each equivalence class are {{em|identified}} or "glued together" for forming a new topological space. For example, identifying the points of a [[sphere]] that belong to the same [[diameter]] produces the [[projective plane]] as a quotient space.

==Definition==

Let <math>X</math> be a [[topological space]], and let <math>\sim</math> be an [[equivalence relation]] on <math>X.</math> The [[quotient set]] <math>Y = X/{\sim}</math> is the set of [[equivalence class]]es of elements of <math>X.</math> The equivalence class of <math>x \in X</math> is denoted <math>[x].</math>   

The construction of <math>Y</math> defines a canonical [[Surjective function|surjection]] <math>q:X\to Y, x\mapsto[x].</math>
As discussed below, <math>q</math> is a quotient mapping, commonly called the canonical quotient map, or canonical projection map, associated to <math>X/{\sim}.</math>

The '''quotient space''' under <math>\sim</math> is the set <math>Y</math> equipped with the '''quotient topology''', whose [[open set]]s are those [[subset]]s <math display="inline">U \subseteq Y</math> whose [[preimage]] <math>q^{-1}(U)</math> is [[Open set|open]].  In other words, <math>U</math> is open in the quotient topology on <math>X / {\sim}</math> if and only if {{Nowrap|<math display=inline>\{ x \in X : [x] \in U \}</math>}} is open in <math>X.</math>  Similarly, a subset <math>S \subseteq Y</math> is [[Closed set|closed]] if and only if <math>\{ x \in X : [x] \in S \}</math> is closed in <math>X.</math>

The quotient topology is the [[final topology]] on the quotient set, with respect to the map <math>x \mapsto [x].</math>

==Quotient map==

A map <math>f : X \to Y</math> is a '''quotient map''' (sometimes called an '''identification map'''{{sfn|Brown|2006|p=103}}) if it is [[Surjective function|surjective]] and <math>Y</math> is equipped with the [[final topology]] induced by <math>f.</math>  The latter condition admits two more-elementary formulations: a subset <math>V \subseteq Y</math> is open (closed) if and only if <math>f^{-1}(V)</math> is open (resp. closed).  Every quotient map is continuous but not every continuous map is a quotient map. 

'''Saturated sets'''

A subset <math>S</math> of <math>X</math> is called '''[[Saturated set|saturated]]''' (with respect to <math>f</math>) if it is of the form <math>S = f^{-1}(T)</math> for some set <math>T,</math> which is true if and only if <math>f^{-1}(f(S)) = S.</math>
The assignment <math>T \mapsto f^{-1}(T)</math> establishes a [[Bijection|one-to-one correspondence]] (whose inverse is <math>S \mapsto f(S)</math>) between subsets <math>T</math> of <math>Y = f(X)</math> and saturated subsets of <math>X.</math> 
With this terminology, a surjection <math>f : X \to Y</math> is a quotient map if and only if for every {{em|saturated}} subset <math>S</math> of <math>X,</math> <math>S</math> is open in <math>X</math> if and only if <math>f(S)</math> is open in <math>Y.</math> 
In particular, open subsets of <math>X</math> that are {{em|not}} saturated have no impact on whether the function <math>f</math> is a quotient map (or, indeed, continuous: a function <math>f : X \to Y</math> is continuous if and only if, for every saturated <math display="inline">S\subseteq X</math> such that <math>f(S)</math> is open in {{Nowrap|<math display=inline>f(X)</math>,}} the set <math>S</math> is open in {{Nowrap|<math display=inline>X</math>).}}  

Indeed, if <math>\tau</math> is a [[Topology (structure)|topology]] on <math>X</math> and <math>f : X \to Y</math> is any map, then the set <math>\tau_f</math> of all <math>U \in \tau</math> that are saturated subsets of <math>X</math> forms a topology on <math>X.</math> If <math>Y</math> is also a topological space then <math>f : (X, \tau) \to Y</math> is a quotient map (respectively, [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]]) if and only if the same is true of <math>f : \left(X, \tau_f\right) \to Y.</math>

'''Quotient space of fibers characterization'''

Given an [[equivalence relation]] <math>\,\sim\,</math> on <math>X,</math> denote the [[equivalence class]] of a point <math>x \in X</math> by <math>[x] := \{z \in X : z \sim x\}</math> and let <math>X /{\sim} := \{[x] : x \in X\}</math> denote the set of equivalence classes. The map <math>q : X \to X /{\sim}</math> that sends points to their [[equivalence class]]es (that is, it is defined by <math>q(x) := [x]</math> for every <math>x \in X</math>) is called {{em|the canonical map}}. It is a [[surjective map]] and for all <math>a, b \in X,</math> <math>a \,\sim\, b</math> if and only if <math>q(a) = q(b);</math> consequently, <math>q(x) = q^{-1}(q(x))</math> for all <math>x \in X.</math> In particular, this shows that the set of equivalence class <math>X /{\sim}</math> is exactly the set of fibers of the canonical map <math>q.</math>
If <math>X</math> is a topological space then giving <math>X /{\sim}</math> the quotient topology induced by <math>q</math> will make it into a quotient space and make <math>q : X \to X /{\sim}</math> into a quotient map. 
[[Up to]] a [[homeomorphism]], this construction is representative of all quotient spaces; the precise meaning of this is now explained. 

Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be a surjection between topological spaces (not yet assumed to be continuous or a quotient map) and declare for all <math>a, b \in X</math> that <math>a \,\sim\, b</math> if and only if <math>f(a) = f(b).</math> Then <math>\,\sim\,</math> is an equivalence relation on <math>X</math> such that for every <math>x \in X,</math> <math>[x] = f^{-1}(f(x)),</math> which implies that <math>f([x])</math> (defined by <math>f([x]) = \{ \,f(z)\, : z \in [x]\}</math>) is a [[singleton set]]; denote the unique element in <math>f([x])</math> by <math>\hat{f}([x])</math> (so by definition, <math>f([x]) = \{ \,\hat{f}([x])\, \}</math>). 
The assignment <math>[x] \mapsto \hat{f}([x])</math> defines a [[bijection]] <math>\hat{f} : X /{\sim} \;\to\; Y</math> between the fibers of <math>f</math> and points in <math>Y.</math> 
Define the map <math>q : X \to X / {\sim}</math> as above (by <math>q(x) := [x]</math>) and give <math>X / {\sim}</math> the quotient topology induced by <math>q</math> (which makes <math>q</math> a quotient map). These maps are related by: <math display=block>f = \hat{f} \circ q \quad \text{ and } \quad q = \hat{f}^{-1} \circ f.</math> 
From this and the fact that <math>q : X \to X / {\sim}</math> is a quotient map, it follows that <math>f : X \to Y</math> is continuous if and only if this is true of <math>\hat{f} : X / {\sim} \;\to\; Y.</math> Furthermore, <math>f : X \to Y</math> is a quotient map if and only if <math>\hat{f} : X / {\sim} \;\to\; Y</math> is a [[homeomorphism]] (or equivalently, if and only if both <math>\hat{f}</math> and its inverse are continuous). 

===Related definitions===

A '''{{visible anchor|hereditarily quotient map|Hereditarily quotient map|Hereditarily quotient}}''' is a surjective map <math>f : X \to Y</math> with the property that for every subset <math>T \subseteq Y,</math> the restriction <math>f\big\vert_{f^{-1}(T)} ~:~ f^{-1}(T) \to T</math> is also a quotient map. 
There exist quotient maps that are not hereditarily quotient.

==Examples==

* '''Gluing'''.  Topologists talk of gluing points together.  If <math>X</math> is a topological space, gluing the points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> in <math>X</math> means considering the quotient space obtained from the equivalence relation <math>a \sim b</math> if and only if <math>a = b</math> or <math>a = x, b = y</math> (or <math>a = y, b = x</math>).
* Consider the unit square <math>I^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]</math> and the equivalence relation <math>\sim</math> generated by the requirement that all boundary points be equivalent, thus identifying all boundary points to a single equivalence class. Then <math>I^2 / \sim</math> is [[homeomorphic]] to the [[sphere]] <math>S^2.</math>
[[File:Collapsing a subspace.svg|thumb|For example, <math>[0,1]/\{0,1\}</math> is homeomorphic to the circle <math>S^1.</math>]]
*'''[[Adjunction space]]'''. More generally, suppose <math>X</math> is a space and <math>A</math> is a [[Subspace (topology)|subspace]] of <math>X.</math> One can identify all points in <math>A</math> to a single equivalence class and leave points outside of <math>A</math> equivalent only to themselves. The resulting quotient space is denoted <math>X/A.</math> The 2-sphere is then homeomorphic to a [[Unit disc|closed disc]] with its boundary identified to a single point: <math>D^2 / \partial{D^2}.</math>
* Consider the set <math>\R</math> of [[real number]]s with the ordinary topology, and write <math>x \sim y</math> [[if and only if]] <math>x - y</math> is an [[integer]]. Then the quotient space <math>X / {\sim}</math> is [[homeomorphic]] to the [[unit circle]] <math>S^1</math> via the homeomorphism which sends the equivalence class of <math>x</math> to <math>\exp(2 \pi i x).</math>
* A generalization of the previous example is the following: Suppose a [[topological group]] <math>G</math> [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] continuously on a space <math>X.</math> One can form an equivalence relation on <math>X</math> by saying points are equivalent if and only if they lie in the same [[Orbit (group theory)|orbit]]. The quotient space under this relation is called the '''orbit space''', denoted <math>X / G.</math> In the previous example <math>G = \Z</math> acts on <math>\R</math> by translation. The orbit space <math>\R / \Z</math> is homeomorphic to <math>S^1.</math>
**''Note'': The notation <math>\R / \Z</math> is somewhat ambiguous. If <math>\Z</math> is understood to be a group acting on <math>\R</math> via addition, then the [[Quotient group|quotient]] is the circle. However, if <math>\Z</math> is thought of as a topological subspace of <math>\R</math> (that is identified as a single point) then the quotient <math>\{ \Z \} \cup \{ \,\{r\} : r \in \R \setminus \Z \}</math> (which is [[Bijection|identifiable]] with the set <math>\{ \Z \} \cup (\R \setminus \Z)</math>) is a countably infinite [[bouquet of circles]] joined at a single point <math>\Z.</math>
* This next example shows that it is in general {{em|not}} true that if <math>q : X \to Y</math> is a quotient map then every [[convergent sequence]] (respectively, every [[Convergent net|convergent]] [[Net (mathematics)|net]]) in <math>Y</math> has a [[Lift (mathematics)|lift]] (by <math>q</math>) to a convergent sequence (or [[convergent net]]) in <math>X.</math> Let <math>X = [0, 1]</math> and <math>\,\sim ~=~ \{ \,\{ 0, 1 \} \, \} ~\cup~ \left\{ \{ x \} : x \in (0, 1) \, \right\}.</math> Let <math>Y :=  X / {\sim}</math> and let <math>q : X \to  X / {\sim}</math> be the quotient map <math>q(x) := [x],</math> so that <math>q(0) = q(1) = \{ 0, 1 \}</math> and <math>q(x) = \{ x \}</math> for every <math>x \in (0, 1).</math> The map <math>h :  X / {\sim}\to S^1 \subseteq \Complex</math> defined by <math>h([x]) := e^{2 \pi i x}</math> is well-defined (because <math>e^{2 \pi i (0)} = 1 = e^{2 \pi i (1)}</math>) and a [[homeomorphism]]. Let <math>I = \N</math> and let <math>a_{\bull} := \left(a_i\right)_{i \in I} \text{ and } b_{\bull} := \left(b_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> be any sequences (or more generally, any nets) valued in <math>(0, 1)</math> such that <math>a_{\bull} \to 0 \text{ and } b_{\bull} \to 1</math> in <math>X = [0, 1].</math> Then the sequence <math display=block>y_1 := q\left(a_1\right), y_2 := q\left(b_1\right), y_3 := q\left(a_2\right), y_4 := q\left(b_2\right), \ldots</math> converges to <math>[0] = [1]</math> in <math> X / {\sim}</math> but there does not exist any convergent lift of this sequence by the quotient map <math>q</math> (that is, there is no sequence <math>s_{\bull} = \left(s_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> in <math>X</math> that both converges to some <math>x \in X</math> and satisfies <math>y_i = q\left(s_i\right)</math> for every <math>i \in I</math>). This counterexample can be generalized to [[Net (mathematics)|nets]] by letting <math>(A, \leq)</math> be any [[directed set]], and making <math>I := A \times \{ 1, 2 \}</math> into a net by declaring that for any <math>(a, m), (b, n) \in I,</math> <math>(m, a) \; \leq \; (n, b)</math> holds if and only if both (1) <math>a \leq b,</math> and (2) if <math>a = b \text{ then } m \leq n;</math> then the <math>A</math>-indexed net defined by letting <math>y_{(a, m)}</math> equal <math>a_i \text{ if } m = 1</math> and equal to <math>b_i \text{ if } m = 2</math> has no lift (by <math>q</math>) to a convergent <math>A</math>-indexed net in <math>X = [0, 1].</math>

==Properties==

Quotient maps <math>q : X \to Y</math> are characterized among surjective maps by the following property: if <math>Z</math> is any topological space and <math>f : Y \to Z</math> is any function, then <math>f</math> is continuous if and only if <math>f \circ q</math> is continuous.

[[Image:QuotientSpace-01.svg|center|Characteristic property of the quotient topology]]

The quotient space <math>X /{\sim}</math> together with the quotient map <math>q : X \to X /{\sim}</math> is characterized by the following [[universal property]]: if <math>g : X \to Z</math> is a continuous map such that <math>a \sim b</math> implies <math>g(a) = g(b)</math> for all <math>a, b \in X,</math> then there exists a unique continuous map <math>f : X / {\sim} \to Z</math> such that <math>g = f \circ q.</math> In other words, the following diagram commutes:

[[File:Universal Property of Quotient Spaces.svg|center|frameless]]

One says that <math>g</math> ''descends to the quotient'' for expressing this, that is that it factorizes through the quotient space. The continuous maps defined on <math>X /{\sim}</math> are, therefore, precisely those maps which arise from continuous maps defined on <math>X</math> that respect the equivalence relation (in the sense that they send equivalent elements to the same image). This criterion is copiously used when studying quotient spaces.

Given a continuous surjection <math>q : X \to Y</math> it is useful to have criteria by which one can determine if <math>q</math> is a quotient map. Two sufficient criteria are that <math>q</math> be [[Open map|open]] or [[Closed map|closed]]. Note that these conditions are only [[Sufficient condition|sufficient]], not [[Necessary condition|necessary]]. It is easy to construct examples of quotient maps that are neither open nor closed. For topological groups, the quotient map is open.

==Compatibility with other topological notions==

===Separation properties===
In general, quotient spaces are ill-behaved with respect to [[separation axioms]]. The separation properties of <math>X</math> need not be inherited by <math> X / {\sim}</math> and <math> X / {\sim}</math> may have separation properties not shared by <math>X.</math>

<math>X/{\sim}</math> is a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] if and only if every equivalence class of <math>\sim</math> is closed in <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Engelking|1989|p=94}}
As an example, consider the space <math>X=[0,1]</math> and its subset <math>A=[0,1),</math> which is not closed.  The quotient space <math>X/A</math> obtained by identifying all points of <math>A</math> to a single point is homeomorphic to [[Sierpiński space]], which is not T<sub>1</sub>.

For <math>X/{\sim}</math> to be a [[Hausdorff space]], a stronger condition is required: <math>\sim</math> must be a closed equivalence relation, in the sense that the set <math>R=\{(x,y)\in X\times X:x\sim y\}</math> must be closed in the [[product space]] <math>X\times X.</math>{{sfn|Willard|2004|loc=Theorem 13.10}}
This condition is not sufficient though.  For example, if <math>A</math> is a closed set in a Hausdorff space <math>X,</math> the equivalence relation that identifies all points of <math>A</math> to a single point is the set <math>R=(A\times A)\cup\Delta</math> (with <math>\Delta</math> being the diagonal in <math>X\times X</math>), which is closed in <math>X\times X.</math>
But the quotient space <math>X/{\sim}</math> will not be Hausdorff if <math>X</math> is not [[regular space|regular]] and <math>A</math> is a closed set that cannot be separated by open sets from a point <math>x\notin A.</math>

If the quotient map is [[Open map|open]], then <math> X/{\sim}</math> is Hausdorff if and only if the relation <math>\sim</math> is closed in <math>X \times X.</math>{{sfn|Willard|2004|loc=Theorem 13.12}}

Some separation properties are preserved under certain conditions.  In particular,
* If <math>X</math> is a [[T4 space|T<sub>4</sub> space]] (i.e., normal Hausdorff) and the quotient map is [[closed map|closed]], then <math>X/{\sim}</math> is also T<sub>4</sub>.{{sfn|Engelking|1989|loc=Theorem 1.5.20}}
* If <math>X</math> is a [[T6 space|T<sub>6</sub> space]] (i.e., perfectly normal Hausdorff) and the quotient map is closed, then <math>X/{\sim}</math> is also T<sub>6</sub>.{{sfn|Engelking|1989|loc=Theorem 1.5.20}}
* If <math>X</math> is compact Hausdorff, the following are equivalent: (i) <math>X/{\sim}</math> is Hausdorff; (ii) the quotient map is closed; (iii) the relation <math>\sim</math> is closed in <math>X\times X.</math>{{sfn|tom Dieck|2008|loc=Proposition 1.4.4}}{{sfn|Willard|2004|loc=Problem 17N (2)}}

===Connectedness===
* If a space is connected or [[path connected]], then so are all its quotient spaces.
* A quotient space of a [[simply connected]] or [[contractible]] space need not share those properties.

===Compactness===
* If a space is compact, then so are all its quotient spaces.
* A quotient space of a [[locally compact]] space need not be locally compact.

===Dimension===
* The [[topological dimension]] of a quotient space can be more (as well as less) than the dimension of the original space; [[space-filling curve]]s provide such examples.
